summary: Tanishq jewellery, Titan and Fastrack watches, Titan Eye+ eyewear and other lifestyle offerings sit within one group, with different customer needs and economics.
description: Titan develops and sells jewellery, watches, eyewear and other lifestyle products through stores and online channels. Design, trust, sourcing, manufacturing and retail execution support these offerings. Jewellery purchases involve valuable metal and stones, while a watch or an optical order has a different cost structure and buying occasion.
money: Titan earns revenue by selling its products through the relevant retail, distribution and online arrangements. Materials, design, manufacturing, retail costs, marketing, product mix and money tied up in stock affect what remains from those sales.
customers: People buying jewellery for weddings, gifting or personal use, customers choosing watches or eyewear, and shoppers buying clothing, fragrances and accessories. Store operators and other businesses can also be part of the route to the final customer.
drivers: Gold prices and quantities, jewellery mix, buying occasions, store productivity, brand investment and inventory funding. Smaller divisions and acquired businesses can grow at different rates and contribute very different earnings.

groups.title: Jewellery
groups.examples: Tanishq, Mia, Zoya and CaratLane serve different jewellery occasions and customer preferences; Damas joins the group through its acquisition.
groups.explanation: The bill reflects metal, stones, design and other charges. A rise in gold prices can lift the rupee sale without the same increase in grams or purchases. Recognising a brand does not reveal its individual profit.

groups.title: Watches and wearables
groups.examples: Titan, Fastrack, Sonata and other watch ranges, plus wearable offerings and watch retail formats such as Helios.
groups.explanation: Design, price bands, distribution and changing preferences matter. Analog watches and smart wearables compete with different alternatives; their growth should be read separately where disclosed.

groups.title: Eyecare
groups.examples: Titan Eye+ and the related eyewear range offer spectacles, frames, lenses and optical retail services.
groups.explanation: The purchase combines product selection with an optical service experience. Store productivity, product mix, quality and repeat relationships affect the business; this page does not assess clinical outcomes.

groups.title: Newer lifestyle offerings
groups.examples: Taneira Indian dresswear, SKINN fragrances, IRTH bags and other accessories.
groups.explanation: These involve different buying occasions and competitors. New stores and familiar branding can support demand, but small categories still have to cover stock, people, marketing and retail costs.

basics.title: A brand is different from a reported segment
basics.text: Tanishq is a brand; Jewellery is a reported business segment that bundles activities and brands. The consolidated accounts also include controlled subsidiaries under the applicable rules. A segment result is therefore not a profit statement for a particular ring or watch.

basics.title: A store network can use different commercial arrangements
basics.text: A branded outlet can operate under company or franchise arrangements. Footprint describes customer access, not necessarily property ownership or identical economics at every outlet. Check the channel and ownership definition before comparing store counts.

steps.title: Understand the buying occasion
steps.text: Choose designs, ranges and price points for weddings, gifting, everyday use or other customer needs.

steps.title: Source, make and control quality
steps.text: Arrange the appropriate metal, stones, components or finished products, then manage manufacturing, sourcing and quality under the relevant business arrangement.

steps.title: Make the offering available
steps.text: Hold the right range and sizes across the relevant stores and online channels. Stock that is available but not selling still needs funding.

steps.title: Complete the sale and support the customer
steps.text: Earn the purchase through design, trust, pricing and service, while managing the associated costs and any exchange, repair or after-sales obligations.

specifics.title: Gold value, product quantity and value added are different
specifics.text: More rupees of jewellery sales need not mean more grams sold. Higher gold prices, larger purchases, product mix and more transactions can change sales differently. Making charges are not pure profit: design, production, distribution and running costs still have to be covered.

specifics.title: Jewellery inventory has a financing side
specifics.text: Metal and finished jewellery tie up value before a customer purchases them. Read stock turnover, borrowings, gold-on-loan arrangements and hedging disclosures together. Hedging manages specified price exposure; it does not guarantee customer demand, remove funding costs or make all gold-price changes harmless.

specifics.title: Mix and store maturity affect the result
specifics.text: Plain-metal and studded jewellery, analog watches and wearables, and mature versus newer stores can have different costs and sales patterns. A higher-priced product is not automatically more profitable. Evaluate established-store performance, category mix and investment rather than relying only on footprint expansion.

watch: Is jewellery growth coming from gold prices or customer demand?
Separate value growth from quantity, ticket size, transactions and product mix.

Read the jewellery review for the stated measures of buyers, bill size, grams or volume, where disclosed. Compare the same periods and definitions. Gold inflation can raise revenue while customers choose lighter items; demand cannot be read from the sales value alone.
Does the product mix support the earnings reported?
Look at plain versus studded jewellery and analog watches versus wearables where disclosed.

Read the relevant segment commentary and reported result together. Do not substitute one brand’s positioning for a segment margin. Check pricing, discounts, marketing and exceptional or unusual effects before explaining a profit change.
Are inventory and financing being managed together?
Understand how much money the range requires and what price exposure remains.

Compare inventory, cash flow, borrowings and gold-on-loan or hedging notes. Identify what each arrangement covers and when obligations fall due. A hedge or customer advance is not evidence that the business needs no capital or faces no risk.
Are additional stores and newer businesses earning useful returns?
Distinguish opening a location from generating sustainable profit and cash.

Compare established-store trends, new-store maturity, channel arrangements and capital spending. Read Watches, Eyecare and Others individually. A familiar group brand or an expanding network does not establish that each business is profitable.
Are acquisitions and reporting measures comparable?
Keep standalone, consolidated, acquisition dates and bullion definitions consistent.

The FY 2025–26 presentation includes Damas after acquisition from the final quarter and excludes bullion and digi-gold from certain headline income figures. Compare the same scope and period with the statutory segment table, which uses a different revenue definition. Acquired revenue is different from growth in existing operations.
risks: Gold prices change affordability and stock needs
Rising metal prices can increase the money needed for stock and lead customers to buy differently. Pricing, funding and hedging address different parts of the exposure.
Trust or execution fails at the point of purchase
Product quality, purity, design, service and fulfilment affect customer trust. A problem at an outlet or in a range needs to be assessed for its actual scope.
Expansion costs arrive before adequate demand
New stores, new categories and acquisitions require stock, people and investment. Slower maturity or weak demand can delay returns.
Local jewellers, national brands and online sellers compete on design, trust, price and convenience. Watches, eyewear and newer lifestyle categories each face their own alternatives.
context: An acquisition changes what a comparison includes

Titan’s FY 2025–26 results describe the completed majority acquisition of Damas and its inclusion from the acquisition period. This adds a business and customer base to the group. To understand underlying growth, distinguish acquired operations from the performance of the businesses already included in the earlier comparison.
quiz: Can higher jewellery revenue alone prove that Titan sold more jewellery by weight?

No. Higher gold prices, different stone or product mix, larger bills, more customers and acquired operations can all change revenue. Read the quantity and transaction measures the company actually discloses, then check the matching profit and cash measures.
sources: FY 2025–26 earnings presentation and measurement notes

financialNotes.title: The watch name does not describe the largest earnings source
financialNotes.text: In the verified FY 2025–26 consolidated segment statement, Jewellery reports ₹79,660 crore of revenue and ₹7,209 crore segment profit; Watches reports ₹5,267 crore and ₹824 crore respectively. These are segment measures before company-level finance costs, exceptional items and tax, not individual-brand profits.

financialNotes.title: Check which gold sales the headline includes
financialNotes.text: The statutory table includes other income, bullion and digi-gold sales. The earnings presentation excludes bullion and digi-gold from specified headline total-income figures. These different definitions should not be treated as conflicting versions of the same sales measure or mixed to calculate a margin.

financialNotes.title: Keep corporate costs and cash in view
financialNotes.text: The corporate unallocated line has a ₹201 crore loss, reducing the combined segment result. The Others row is not a profit measure for every new lifestyle brand. Read the reconciliation, inventory funding, acquisition payments and cash flow before treating the segment total as cash available to shareholders.
